clue.text: Notice tenor has taken part in musical piece

indicators.note: in tells us the abbreviation for part sits inside the word for notice

parts.note: to notice something is to see it
T is a common abbreviation for tenor in vocal scores

explanation.surface: A notice says a tenor has been given a role in a stage musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a noun (a poster), but it is the verb SEE. 'In' puts PT inside SEE, giving SEPTE, and T follows; 'has taken' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of music written for seven players or singers is called a septet.

clue.text: Provide drink before work

indicators.note: before puts the drink word ahead of the work word

parts.note: to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls
to ply is to work at a trade

explanation.surface: Someone advises having a drink before starting work.
explanation.definitionFit: To supply is to furnish or give what is needed.

clue.text: Maybe fine drive round Northern Ireland

indicators.note: round means the drive word goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: to push is to drive forward

explanation.surface: Perhaps a fine awaits after a drive around Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' shows the definition is an example: a fine is one kind of penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fining someone is one way to penalise them for wrongdoing.

clue.text: Former partner likely to be summoned in court is nervous

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner

parts.words: likely to be summoned in court
parts.note: to cite is to summon someone to appear in court, so a person liable to that is citable

explanation.surface: An ex-spouse expecting to be called to court is on edge.
explanation.definitionFit: An excitable person is easily agitated, highly strung and jumpy.

clue.text: Tool one wants to get repaired

indicators.note: something repaired is put back together, so the letters of these words are reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A handyman's tool needs fixing, as anyone would want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repaired' rearranges the eight letters of ONE WANTS; 'to get' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenon saw is a small fine-toothed carpentry saw used for cutting joints.

clue.text: Ex-BR employees, retrained by Virgin, sneered

indicators.note: retrained suggests the letters are trained into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Former British Rail staff sneer at being retrained by the Virgin train company.
explanation.walkthrough: BR is British Rail, the old nationalised railway; Virgin Trains took over some of its routes. 'Retrained' shuffles VIRGIN SNEERED.
explanation.definitionFit: Engine drivers worked for the state railway, so former British Rail staff included them.

clue.text: Unopened drink put to cool

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Unopened drink put to cool' (2,3) is cut short: the blog parses it as (T)ONIC + the last letter of FRIDGE, but the held clue has no word for fridge or its final letter.

clue.text: Fuel fit for storing in the ground

indicators.note: storing in says the ground word holds the fit word inside it

parts.note: soil is ground or earth
hale means healthy and fit

explanation.surface: A fuel suitable for keeping underground.
explanation.walkthrough: HALE goes inside SOIL. 'For' and 'the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Shale oil is a petroleum extracted from oil-bearing shale rock, used as a fuel.

clue.text: Chain store reportedly no longer supplying winter wear

indicators.note: reportedly says the nickname is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Woolies was the nickname of Woolworths, a British chain of high-street shops

explanation.surface: A chain store, it is said, no longer stocks winter clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer supplying' describes Woolworths, the British chain that closed in 2009, and adds nothing to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Woollen garments such as jumpers and cardigans are worn in cold weather.

clue.text: Filled with anxiety, seeing old man committing crime

parts.note: old man is informal for father, PA
nicking is British slang for stealing, the crime here

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious on finding their father in the act of a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: NICK is everyday British slang for steal (and also for arrest); 'seeing' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Being gripped by sudden fear or alarm is what panic means, so the participle fits a state of anxiety.

clue.text: Angry about new Tory faction being uncaring

indicators.note: about means the angry word goes around the other pieces

parts.note: irate means angry
CON is short for Conservative, the Tory party in Britain
a side is a faction or party in a dispute

explanation.surface: Indignant at a new Conservative group showing indifference.
explanation.walkthrough: N + CON + SIDE goes inside IRATE, split as I...RATE. 'Being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An inconsiderate person shows thoughtless disregard for others' feelings.

clue.text: Coming out of Florida, holidaymakers see a different part of the US

definitions.text: a different part of the US

indicators.note: the letters emerge from inside these two words, running across the comma between them

explanation.surface: Tourists leaving Florida travel on to see another region of America.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits in floRIDA, HOlidaymakers... read from the I: flor-IDA HO-lidaymakers. 'See' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A northwestern state of America is certainly another part of the country from Florida.

clue.text: Catalogue includes unknown composer's name

indicators.note: includes means the catalogue word holds the unknown letter within it

parts.note: a catalogue is a list
Z is a mathematical unknown, like x and y

explanation.surface: A record catalogue lists the name of a composer nobody has heard of.
explanation.walkthrough: Mathematical unknowns are x, y and z, so 'unknown' supplies Z, which sits inside LIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was the Hungarian Romantic composer and piano virtuoso.

clue.text: Fish that's gone bad in basket

indicators.note: in places the jumbled word within the basket word

parts.note: a creel is an angler's wicker basket for fish

indicators.note: gone bad means spoiled, so the letters of gone are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: A fish left in the angler's basket has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' turns GONE into ONGE, and 'in' puts that inside CREEL. 'That's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A conger is a large marine eel, a type of sea fish.

clue.text: Order introduced into African country by English monk

indicators.note: introduced into says the word for order goes inside the country's name

parts.note: Benin is a country in West Africa
an edict is an official order or decree

explanation.surface: An English monk brings a decree into an African nation.
explanation.walkthrough: EDICT goes into BENIN to give BENEDICTIN, then E follows; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Benedictine is a member of the religious order founded by St Benedict.

clue.text: Maybe Europe wants troops out of Gulf

indicators.note: out of means the abbreviation is taken away from the troops word

parts.note: a contingent is a body of troops sent to join a larger force
G is an abbreviation for gulf, as on maps

explanation.surface: Europe perhaps wants soldiers withdrawn from the Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of' looks like 'away from' but removes G from CONTINGENT. 'Maybe' marks Europe as one example; 'wants' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Europe is one of the world's seven great landmasses.

clue.text: Today's dishes, almost all coated in exotic spices

indicators.note: coated in puts the shortened word inside the jumbled spices
exotic suggests the letters of spices are made strange and rearranged
almost means the word all loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Today's menu dishes are nearly all covered in foreign spices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exotic' rearranges SPICES into SPECIS; 'almost' cuts ALL to AL; 'coated in' puts AL inside: SPECI-AL-S.
explanation.definitionFit: Specials are the chef's dishes of the day added to a restaurant menu.

clue.text: Gosh! Grass comes up before end of April in one part of Britain

indicators.note: before places the reversed grass ahead of that letter

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like gosh

indicators.note: in a down clue comes up means the grass word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a lawn is an area of grass

indicators.note: end of takes the last letter of April

explanation.surface: Amazement as the grass grows before April is out somewhere in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes up' turns LAWN into NWAL; 'end of' gives L from April. Cornwall is the county at Britain's southwestern tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornwall is a county forming the southwest peninsula of England.

clue.text: Open Chianti specially for language expert

indicators.note: specially suggests these letters are arranged in a special new way

explanation.surface: Someone uncorks a bottle of Italian red wine for a visiting linguist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Specially' rearranges the eleven letters of OPEN CHIANTI; 'for' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A phonetician studies speech sounds, a branch of linguistics.

clue.text: Democrat checked by US Vice President as ordered

indicators.note: checked by means the Democrat letter is held in by the name around it

parts.note: Joe Biden was vice president under Obama when this was set
D is the abbreviation for a Democrat in US politics

explanation.surface: A Democrat is reined in by the US Vice President as instructed.
explanation.walkthrough: D goes inside BIDEN. 'As' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bidden is the old past participle of bid, meaning commanded or told to do something.

clue.text: I'm accompanying maiden in fling, a sort of dance

indicators.note: in puts those pieces inside the fling word

parts.note: to shy is to fling or throw

indicators.note: accompanying sets the two short pieces side by side

parts.note: I'm gives the letters IM
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: Someone dances a fling with a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' looks like a romance or the Highland fling dance, but is the verb SHY.
explanation.definitionFit: The shimmy is a jazz-age dance with shaking of the shoulders.

clue.text: Worker one's seen entering church is from far eastern city

indicators.note: entering means the worker and one's pieces go inside the church abbreviation

parts.note: CE stands for Church of England
an ant is the classic worker insect in crosswords
one's is read as the word ones

explanation.surface: A labourer is seen going into a church, arriving from a city in the Far East.
explanation.walkthrough: ANT + ONES goes inside CE. 'Is' and 'seen' are links; the definition is adjectival.
explanation.definitionFit: Cantonese describes people or things from Canton, now Guangzhou, in southern China.

clue.text: Rise of Communist party more unexpected

indicators.note: in a down clue rise means the pieces are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: red is a familiar term for a communist
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: The rise of a Communist party was rather surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: RED DO read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something odder is stranger or more peculiar than expected.

clue.text: Language used by Kashmiri shepherds

indicators.note: used by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A tongue spoken by herders in Kashmir.
explanation.walkthrough: The run straddles the two words: kashm-IRI SH-epherds.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish Gaelic is the Celtic tongue of Ireland.

clue.text: Medal perhaps presented finally at end of a conflict

indicators.note: at end of says this letter comes after the a and the conflict word

parts.note: a war is a conflict

indicators.note: finally takes only the final letter of the word presented

explanation.surface: A medal is handed out when a war finally ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' gives D from presented, which 'at end of' places after A WAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A medal is one example of a prize or honour given in recognition.

clue.text: Trams made to whizz round city

indicators.note: whizz round suggests the letters spinning about into a new order

explanation.surface: Trams are made to zip around a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To whizz round' shuffles the nine letters of TRAMS MADE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch capital is famous for its trams.

clue.text: Receiving regular wage? Sadly, after retirement, one goes into the red

indicators.note: retirement means going back, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: alas is an exclamation meaning sadly

indicators.note: goes into puts the numeral inside the word red

parts.note: red taken as itself
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A retired person no longer earning a wage sadly falls into debt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After retirement' turns ALAS into SALA; 'goes into' puts I inside RED to make RIED. 'Sadly' looks like an adverb but is ALAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A salaried worker is paid a fixed regular sum, monthly or annually.

clue.text: Mean scam ending in bankruptcy

parts.note: a sting is a confidence trick or swindle

indicators.note: ending in takes the last letter of the word bankruptcy

explanation.surface: A nasty swindle ends in someone going bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like a verb or noun but is the adjective for tight with money.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingy people are miserly, ungenerous with money.
